title: Should supermarkets stop selling loss leaders?

turns.speaker: Ola
turns.text: Milk is cheaper than bottled water again. Below what it costs to produce, on most estimates.

turns.speaker: Vince
turns.text: Which is deliberate. Milk and bread bring you through the door and the margin is made on everything else in the basket.

turns.speaker: Trish
turns.text: The cost lands on the farmer, though, because the supermarket doesn't absorb it. It pushes it back up the chain.

turns.speaker: Ola
turns.text: And a dairy farmer can't hold milk back for a better price. It's produced daily whether anyone wants it or not.

turns.speaker: Vince
turns.text: So the perishability is what removes their bargaining power entirely.

turns.speaker: Trish
turns.text: France banned selling below cost, and prices on those items rose, which is exactly what it was meant to do.

turns.speaker: Ola
turns.text: Did the farmers actually see it?

turns.speaker: Trish
turns.text: Partially. Some of it stayed in the middle of the chain, which is the usual outcome.

turns.speaker: Vince
turns.text: And meanwhile cheap milk is not a trivial thing for a household counting pennies.

turns.speaker: Ola
turns.text: That's the honest tension. The people helped by the ban and the people hurt by it are both poor.

turns.speaker: Trish
turns.text: Which is why the answer is probably a contract rule rather than a price rule. Guarantee the farmer a cost-plus price and let the shop price how it likes.

turns.speaker: Vince
turns.text: The dairy code does roughly that and it's been slow to bite.

turns.speaker: Ola
turns.text: Slow, but at least it targets the part that's actually broken.

points: Milk is sold below production cost as a loss leader to attract customers.
Supermarkets push the cost up the supply chain rather than absorbing it.
Dairy farmers lack bargaining power because milk is perishable and produced daily.
France's ban on below-cost selling raised prices, though only part of the gain reached farmers.
Ola identifies the tension that cheap milk benefits poor households while low prices harm farmers.
Trish argues contract rules guaranteeing cost-plus prices are better targeted than price rules, as the dairy code attempts.
